text: Distance does the work here that a locked door does in most horror films. Three backpackers stranded, a stretch of Australian outback where the nearest help is a day away, and Greg McLean spends ninety-nine minutes on the gap between those two facts. The cinematography took an award at home, and it is the telling prize: the same wide light that sells the country to visitors is what leaves people visible for miles with nowhere to stand. Then the film narrows. The horizon stops being scenery. It becomes a patient study of a local man who knows the ground, the vehicles and the roads, set against three young people who know none of it, and much of the dread is administrative - a question of who is holding the keys and the map.

A sewing machine arrives in a town that settled the question of Tilly's character long ago. Jocelyn Moorhouse sets this in rural Australia in the 1950s, where a woman who can cut and fit a Paris silhouette holds something like power over her neighbours, because every one of them wants to be looked at. Two hours is a long allowance for a story about hems, and the film fills it by running three things at once: a reconciliation with a mother, a courtship, and a slow settling of accounts. The comedy is broad; the grievance underneath it is not. Every award it took at home went to a performance, which is the fair measure of a picture built out of small-town types who each get one scene in which to be more than that.

The offer is arithmetic: the younger brother hangs unless Charlie Burns finds the older one first and kills him. John Hillcoat puts that bargain in the Australian interior of the 1880s, and the Western's familiar furniture - the badge, the ride out, the wanted man up in the hills - sits differently on ground where the settlement is only decades old and everyone in a collar is sweating through it. The costume award is not decorative information. The clothes are part of the argument: heavy European tailoring worn by men in country that will not have it, insisting on law and drawing rooms where both look absurd. What holds the film is that Charlie is given a real choice rather than a trick, and 104 minutes of heat and dust in which to keep not making it.

The screenplay prize is the detail to notice, because the source is a famous prisoner's account of his own life. Andrew Dominik takes Mark 'Chopper' Read at his word and lets the word curdle: the swagger, the wheedling apology, the running commentary a man keeps up to persuade a room that the violence merely happened to him. A biography, technically, though it behaves more like a monologue with witnesses. Ninety-four minutes, much of it in cells, bars and lounge rooms, and the film never stops to explain why anyone would sit still and listen. It doesn't need to. The performance is the engine - the threat is almost entirely a matter of what he might say next, and everyone else in the frame is visibly calculating how to answer.

A radio telescope stands in the middle of an Australian sheep farm, and for a few days the world's view of men walking on the moon depends on the people minding it. Rob Sitch plays most of this for comedy, and the comedy is local: the shire's pride, the visiting American, the small vanities of a town handed a part in something enormous and anxious to get the catering right. What keeps it from being a sketch is the machinery. The film takes seriously that engineering is done by tired men reading dials, that weather is a technical problem, and that decisions have to be made by someone with a name. A score award came of it at home, and the music earns its keep, since a dish turning in a paddock has to be made to feel like an event.

The case is assigned, and that is the whole of the town's interest in it. A girl is found dead under a bridge on a road outside town; the detective handed the file is Aboriginal, so was she, and the colleagues who might have helped have business elsewhere. Ivan Sen shoots it as much like a Western as a procedural, which is a way of saying it follows one man moving alone through country where everybody already knows him and would rather he stopped asking. Two hours of driving, waiting, and conversation that yields nothing useful. Underneath the shape of an investigation sits a plainer matter: what it costs a man to be the only person in the district treating one death as work that has to be done.

Kenny Smyth delivers portable toilets, and treats the trade as one with standards. Clayton Jacobson follows him from festival grounds to a church social to an industry expo in Nashville, and the method throughout is to take the job at the level of the man doing it: hoses, schedules, customers who are rude because of what he arrives in. The gags land where anyone would expect them to, which hardly matters, since the film's actual subject is a competent employee absorbing small humiliations from relatives and strangers who have decided his work is beneath discussion. The lead performance was honoured at home, which fits. The difficulty here stays invisible: ninety-nine minutes of good humour that never turn Kenny into the punchline.

In 2013 the news carried a brawl on Everest - European climbers, a mob of angry Sherpas - and then moved on. Jennifer Peedom went back for the following season to find out what had actually been at issue, and the choice that shapes the film is a simple turn of the camera: the expedition seen from the side of the men who carry the loads, fix the ropes and cross the same ice again and again while the paying climbers rest. That makes it a film about employment. Who takes the risk, and who is spoken about rather than to. Ninety-six minutes at altitude, on a mountain that allows a crew very little room to arrange a shot. What Peedom's team ended up filming was not the season anyone had planned to document.

A car alarm at three in the morning is, in most lives, something to be endured. Henry Bean follows a man who declines to endure it - who begins going after the noise itself, which means going after other people's property, so that a private irritation becomes an offence with police attached. New York is the only address at which this works, a city dense enough that every grievance is simultaneously a crime against somebody. Ninety-two minutes, unsettled in tone on purpose: the comedy of a reasonable complaint pushed well past reason, the thriller of a man who has stopped negotiating with anyone. The pressure worth watching is that he keeps being, on the narrow technical point, right, and that this is no help to him at all.

Four men ride out into the outback, and the only one who knows where they are is the one with no authority over where they go. Rolf de Heer builds everything on that arrangement: an Aboriginal man accused of killing a white woman, three white men on horseback certain of their errand, and the Indigenous tracker whose reading of the ground they need and cannot check. Ninety minutes, early in the last century, with no town to return to and nothing much to verify. The lead performance, honoured at home, is the sort that lives on withheld information - courtesy that may be strategy, agreement that may be nothing of the kind. Less a manhunt than a long test of which man in the party is actually setting the direction.

Kenzo Okuzaki is sixty-two, a veteran of the New Guinea campaign, and he has decided to establish who ordered the deaths of two privates in his unit. Kazuo Hara follows him to the front doors of old soldiers, and what the camera gets is less an inquiry than a sequence of confrontations: an ambush conducted in the grammar of politeness, an ex-sergeant in his own sitting room asked a question he has spent forty years not answering. The essential fact is that Okuzaki knows the camera is running and uses it. His hosts cannot easily throw out a film crew, and Hara does not pretend to be a bystander to that. Two hours in the small rooms of postwar Japan, where the war is still an unsettled account between individual men.

Every line spoken in this film was written by someone else. Jean-Luc Godard assembled the dialogue entirely from books, across several centuries, and handed it to actors playing a wealthy woman and the drifter she takes up with, so that nobody on screen can produce a sentence of their own. The story runs on money, property and water. What the film pushes forward instead is sound: a European award went to the music, and in a work where every word is borrowed, the score is among the few things that can be called its own. Eighty-nine minutes, made in Switzerland, among the very comfortable, and the doubling that runs through it is offered as a puzzle the film is in no hurry to settle.

Fresh out of a Melbourne jail, Dan is handed back the thing he wanted: an afternoon with Leanne, a drink, friends around him, his own announcement that he is finished with all that. Amiel Courtin-Wilson shoots so close in that the film seems overheard rather than written, and the pull is not suspense about the promise but the amount of tenderness two people can assemble out of very little - a room, a lift somewhere, the ordinary luxury of a weekday together. 104 minutes, and the camera stays with them well past the point where a script would cut. The wager is that a couple with a record between them and nothing much ahead can hold the middle of a film simply by being looked at without condescension.

A woman who has been discarded does not make a scene. She makes an introduction. That is the whole engine of Robert Bresson's film, and eighty-four minutes is a tight allowance for a scheme that depends on nobody hurrying. A society lady steers her former lover toward a young woman whose history she alone knows, and every move is made in the language of favours: an invitation, a courtesy, a kindness with a hook in it. Filed as a romance, it plays as engineering. The discomfort comes from the fact that the two people being managed are behaving well - he is courtly, she is careful - and their sincerity is the raw material somebody else has decided to use. Made in France in 1945, and it never once looks outside the rooms it has chosen.
